Key Characteristics & Etiology: Bacterial infection of leptomeninges; S. pneumoniae and N. meningitidis primary pathogens beyond neonatal period
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Bacterial invasion across blood-brain barrier triggering purulent neutrophilic meningeal inflammation and cerebral edema
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: High fever severe headache photophobia neck stiffness Kernig/Brudzinski signs lethargy; Red Flags: Purpura fulminans focal deficit GCS <13
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: CSF: >1000 WBCs/uL (>85% PMNs) protein >1.0 g/L glucose <0.4 ratio Gram stain/culture; High-dose IV Ceftriaxone + Vancomycin + Dexamethasone

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Hematogenous dissemination of Mycobacterium tuberculosis following primary pulmonary infection
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Dense gelatinous basilar exudate entrapping cranial nerves (III VI VII) and encircling circle of Willis causing vasculitis and stroke
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Subacute prodrome (1-3 weeks fever weight loss) cranial nerve palsies neck stiffness seizures; Red Flags: Coma opisthotonos hemiplegia
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: CSF: 100-500 WBCs/uL (lymphocytes) protein 1-5 g/L glucose <0.3 ratio GeneXpert positive CT basilar enhancement; 12m Anti-TB (RHZE) + IV Dexamethasone

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Seizure associated with fever (>38.0C) in children aged 6 to 60 months without CNS infection or metabolic derangement
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Rapid temperature rise lowers seizure threshold in immature vulnerable developing cerebral cortex
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Simple: generalized <15 min no recurrence in 24h; Complex: focal >15 min or >=2 in 24h; Red Flags: Meningismus prolonged post-ictal state
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: Clinical diagnosis Blood glucose electrolytes LP if meningeal signs or <12m; Reassurance + antipyretics + rescue Buccal Midazolam if >5 min

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Continuous seizure activity lasting >=5 minutes or >=2 discrete seizures without interictal consciousness recovery
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Failure of endogenous GABA-mediated seizure termination mechanisms and excessive NMDA receptor excitation
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Continuous clonic or tonic-clonic convulsions altered sensorium systemic hypoxia hyperthermia metabolic acidosis; Red Flags: Airway compromise
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: Blood glucose VBG EEG monitoring CT brain if focal; Immediate 1st line IV Lorazepam (0.1 mg/kg) or Buccal Midazolam -> 2nd line IV Levetiracetam/Fosphenytoin

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Acute viral necrotizing encephalitis caused by HSV-1 (HSV-2 in neonates)
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Retrograde neurotropic spread along trigeminal nerve causing hemorrhagic necrosis of temporal and inferior frontal lobes
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: High fever behavioral changes focal complex partial seizures altered consciousness CSF RBCs; Red Flags: Temporal lobe herniation coma
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: CSF PCR for HSV-1 DNA CSF RBCs MRI brain temporal lobe hyperintensity/necrosis; Immediate IV Acyclovir (10 mg/kg 8-hourly for 14-21 days)

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Non-progressive motor impairment caused by static brain injury; Spastic diplegia highly linked to preterm PVL
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Ischemic injury to periventricular white matter damaging corticospinal tract fibers supplying lower extremities
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Bilateral lower limb spasticity hyperreflexia ankle clonus scissoring gait persistent primitive reflexes; Red Flags: Progressive neurological loss (not CP)
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: Clinical motor evaluation GMFCS functional staging Brain MRI showing periventricular leukomalacia; Multidisciplinary PT/OT + Baclofen/Botulinum toxin

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Self-limiting non-pyogenic inflammation of hip synovial membrane peaking in children 3-8 years following viral URTI
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Post-viral immune-mediated transient synovial hypertrophy and mild joint effusion
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Acute mild hip pain/limp afebrile or low-grade restricted hip internal rotation/abduction; Red Flags: Severe pain high fever non-weight bearing
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: WBC ESR CRP normal or minimally elevated (Kocher criteria negative) Ultrasound small effusion; Rest + Oral NSAIDs (Ibuprofen) self-resolving 1-2 weeks

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Acute pyogenic bacterial infection of hip joint cavity; Staphylococcus aureus most common pathogen
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Bacterial seeding of synovium leading to purulent joint effusion increased intra-articular pressure and risk of avascular necrosis of femoral head
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Acute severe hip pain complete refusal to bear weight high fever (>=38.5C) hip flexed abducted externally rotated; Red Flags: Joint destruction sepsis
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: Kocher criteria positive (Fever non-weight bearing ESR >40 WBC >12k) Ultrasound joint fluid aspiration; Urgent surgical arthrotomy/drainage + IV Antibiotics

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Displacement of proximal femoral epiphysis relative to femoral neck through physis; Peak in obese boys 10-16 years
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Shearing forces across weakened hypertrophic zone of growth plate during adolescent growth spurt
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Dull knee/thigh/groin pain painful limp obligatory external rotation during passive hip flexion; Red Flags: Acute inability to bear weight (unstable SCFE)
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: AP and frog-leg lateral X-rays of pelvis showing failure of Klein's line; Immediate non-weight bearing + Urgent Percutaneous In-Situ Pin Fixation

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Systemic small-vessel IgA immune-complex vasculitis; Often follows viral URTI or GAS pharyngitis
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Deposition of IgA1 immune complexes in small blood vessels of skin GI tract joints and renal glomeruli
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Non-thrombocytopenic palpable purpura over buttocks/legs arthralgia/arthritis colicky abdominal pain hematuria; Red Flags: Intussusception severe nephritis
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: Normal platelet count urinalysis showing hematuria/proteinuria renal ultrasound; Supportive care + Oral Corticosteroids for severe GI/renal disease

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Chronic idiopathic joint inflammation lasting >=6 weeks in children <16 years; Subtypes: Oligoarticular Polyarticular Systemic (Still's)
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Autoimmune chronic synovial hypertrophy villous proliferation and pannus formation leading to cartilage/bone erosion
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Joint pain morning stiffness swelling reduced range of motion; sJIA: quotidian fever salmon rash organomegaly; Oligo JIA: ANA+ high uveitis risk
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: Elevated ESR/CRP positive ANA (oligo) high ferritin (sJIA) slit-lamp eye exam; NSAIDs + Methotrexate + Biologics (Anti-TNF / Anti-IL-6)

Key Characteristics & Etiology: X-linked recessive muscular dystrophy caused by mutations in the dystrophin gene
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Absence of structural dystrophin protein causing sarcolemmal instability muscle fiber necrosis and replacement by fatty fibrous tissue
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Proximal muscle weakness Gowers sign calf pseudohypertrophy waddling gait wheelchair dependent by 12y; Red Flags: Dilated cardiomyopathy hypoventilation
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: Massively elevated serum Creatine Kinase (CK >10,000 U/L) Genetic testing (dystrophin deletion) Muscle biopsy; Oral Glucocorticoids (Prednisone/Deflazacort)

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Acute post-infectious inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy; Classically triggered 1-3 weeks post Campylobacter jejuni infection
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Molecular mimicry causing autoimmune attack against peripheral nerve myelin sheaths and Schwann cells
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Symmetrical ascending flaccid weakness generalized areflexia paresthesias autonomic dysfunction; Red Flags: Respiratory failure (diaphragmatic palsy)
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: CSF: Albuminocytologic dissociation (marked high protein normal WBC) Nerve conduction studies; IV Immunoglobulin (IVIG 2 g/kg) or Plasmapheresis

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Age-specific epileptic encephalopathy occurring in infants 3-12 months; Etiologies: HIE Tuberous Sclerosis chromosomal anomalies
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Severe generalized cortical dysfunction resulting in sudden flexor/extensor muscle contractions and neurodevelopmental regression
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Epileptic flexor/extensor spasms occurring in clusters upon awakening developmental arrest or loss of skills; Red Flags: Developmental regression
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: EEG showing Hypsarrhythmia (chaotic high-voltage background with multifocal spikes) Brain MRI; First-line treatment: High-dose ACTH or Vigabatrin

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Benign generalized epilepsy peaking between 4-8 years; Strong genetic predisposition
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Thalamocortical circuitry hyper-synchronization generating sudden brief bilateral non-convulsive seizure activity
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Brief (5-10 second) sudden vacant staring spells without post-ictal confusion occurring up to 50 times daily triggered by hyperventilation
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: EEG demonstrating characteristic generalized 3 Hz spike-and-wave discharges; First-line medical therapy: Ethosuximide or Sodium Valproate
